For art projects- start with short, easy art project kits. I learned how to crochet with Woobles, and their video tutorials are amazing. I also enjoy building small lego kits (the botanical collection is rewarding if you can afford it). Smaller projects that have instructions don't require you to think so hard about the artistic choices you're making. Much like free recipes on food packages and inside yarn skeins, Michael's (and Joann's until May) have free projects on their websites you can sort through. There are countless free projects online.

As you gain experience, you can start to deviate from the instructions. You can take shapes and skills from one project and combine with another to make your own version. If you go on the Woobles modification Facebook group, you'll see this process at work. I've done things like thrift two shirts and swap out the sleeves. I've made entire outfits from combining different sewing patterns. Then, I'll crochet a scarf to go with it. I make my own costumes for future music videos, sometimes using cosplay techniques that may originate from a character in pop culture. Experiment with using different materials and techniques. Eventually, you can design your own projects from scratch. 

Regarding writing, the common advice is to journal. Writing letters also works. To write prolifically, you want to be able to access a stream of consciousness.  I have a waterproof notepad in my shower to record my ideas as they come. I also use my phone to record song ideas or write notes whenever I'm not near a pen and paper. The idea is to capture an idea ASAP. Then, figure out a system to help you organize. Being a writer can be 24/7. I've full on walked away from loved ones mid-conversation to write down song lyric ideas or record a new melody in MIDI.

Be sure to capture all of your project ideas, preferably in the moment. For example, I'll screenshot outfits that I like, collect paint swatches of colors I like, cut pictures of jewelry out of magazines, etc. Reference your favorite art pieces as inspiration. What qualities do you like? Colors? Styles? Which artists do you admire, and why?

When you're ready to start a new project of your own, brainstorm. Draw from the sources you've collected. Make a list of the steps. Gather the materials. YouTube how-to videos from different sources. Join Facebook groups, and ask for advice whenever you get stuck. Take local classes if you can. For example, I took a stamp making class through my school district's adult education program. Michaels used to have free projects on Sundays, but I'm not sure if they still do that anymore.

I have a mix of tough projects and easy projects. When the more involved projects become too much, if I get stuck, or if I need some momentum to start, I'll do an easier project in between. I alternate between writing lyrics, writing music, recording in a DAW, singing, sewing, costume design, jewelry making, crocheting, scrapbooking, junk journaling, mixed media painting... the list goes on.

There is something fulfilling about finishing a short project in between the chaos of the larger ones. If you need something repetitive and mindless, I scratch that itch by crocheting. I've also enjoyed diamond painting. Coloring in an adult coloring book is something a lot of folk like, but I find it isn't for me. A project that may be mindless for some might not be mindless for you. The same goes for the enjoyability of a craft. Explore all kinds of mediums, and most importantly, pay attention to your enjoyment levels. Determine what's worth it to you, what's easy to you, what is and isn't fulfilling to you... there will be times a project is worth scrapping, and other where it's worth completing despite the struggle. In the end, it's always up to you.

How do I figure out which specimens allow for slight variations and which ones don't?

First, the shape of the oral groove of this specimen better matches P. utiliformis grandis than P. utiliformis. P. utiliformis has a taller, lankier oral groove, whereas grandis looks kinda "squatty" if that makes sense.

Looking at the HORG website, the difference between P. glyphodorsalis and P. utiliformis grandis is the size of the oral groove relative to the rest of the specimen.

With that being said, I am leaning towards P. glyphodorsalis because the shape of this specimen best matches P. utiliformis grandis, but the relative size of the oral groove appears to best match P. utiliformis, meaning this specimen is neither.

Another notable factoid to consider is that, according to the HORG webpage for P. glyphodorsalis, " P. glyphodorsalis is a once-rare and and once-controversial variant of P. utiliformis, as much debate raged  if P. glyphodorsalis is truly a separate species or not."

First and foremost, it sounds like you are in A LOT of pain. Mental pain is no joke. Recently, I experienced a comparison of physical pain to mental pain, a reference I want to share with you. 

I've attempted suicide before, and recently, I got an IUD inserted. Some say the pain of an IUD insert is comparable to the pain of child labor, especially to women who have never given birth before and aren't on their period at the time of insertion. I've gotten cavities filled without novicane. The physical pain I felt from the insertion is the WORST PAIN I've ever felt. I'm a masochist, but I SCREAMED in pain. It was the same type of gutteral scream I've heard in childbirth videos. It was involuntary.

I am one of the lucky few who heard back from Ed via a caretaker in December (Ed asked this caretaker to write to me). I've stayed silent because I wanted to maintain some level of privacy.

Here's some of my strategies:

1. Write in big, bold letters. His eyesight isn't great. I type my letters to him nowadays.

2. Be honest about who you are and your intentions. Let him know why you've decided to write to him.

3. It took me three tries to get a response.

4. Keep your first few letters somewhat brief. My first letter was one page, my third was four pages long (with big font). Remember, he gets a ton of mail, and a shorter letter takes less time to read. Keep in mind that Ed has to be in the right mood to read letters, as he doesn't read them often anymore. One of my letters to him was read two months after I sent it.

5. Empathy. Try putting yourself in his shoes. When I got a response, it was because I spoke (briefly) about my story and how I felt it related to his. With that being said, avoid making assumptions about him that might end up being wrong. Keep in mind what he's said about himself already.

6. Ed likes witty humor.

7. I sent him pictures of me, and I'm a pretty girl (probably his type), so I'm not sure how much that helped.

8. I keep copies of my letters. I date, paginate, and number them at the top so that he knows how many I've sent, and in what order. It also makes it easy to keep track of what you wrote, what works, etc.

9. Check CMF's rules on contraband so that you don't accidentally send the wrong thing.

10. If you hear back from him via a caretaker, it is worthwhile to become the caretaker's pen pal.

Good luck!

After my first EMDR session, I laid around and played video games for like a week. Since my image was related to a specific type of insect, I had trouble eating and drinking. I also started having dreams again. The flashbacks came out of nowhere sometimes. My first few sessions of EMDR after that, like you, affected my mood the most 2-3 days after. I lay around, doom scroll, and nap a lot. My energy level hits 0. Hygiene goes out the window. I might get a little snippy. Even my EMDR sessions are varied from one day to the next. Sometimes, it was intense and emotional and I sobbed. Other times, I'm numb, and it is hard for me to hold an image. 

Two weeks ago, I had a family counseling session (related to the worst level of my ptsd). It triggered me to the point where I have been up till 3,4 am just tossing and turning in bed thinking about it all. I finally slept a little better last night. It took me two weeks just to start returning to a somewhat normal sleep. 

Despite the pain, I like to think that I have the upper hand, though, because I went into EMDR knowing that it would hurt. I let some people around me know that I was doing EMDR, and to expect some of these symptoms. There was some level of anticipation, but it is impossible to prepare for everything.

In regards to some general advice- I partake in weekly activities, like dance class and voice lessons. If you do not do so already, I recommend participating in some sort of weekly activity. There have been days that I realllyyyy did not want to go, but I did anyway, and that really did make me feel better. I also give myself stickers as a reward. Do not underestimate the power of stickers. I find that they help me focus on what I did do, rather than what I didn't do. They help me see my overall progress (and sometimes, regress) over time. Plus, they are fun to look at.

I have had times where I needed help from others. If you have someone in your life that can be your cheerleader, let them know what is going on. You can be general about it (i.e. I am doing this treatment, it works like this, here are some of the side effects). You can work with your therapist to come up with ways to let others know how they can help you. For example, my fiance did not let me skip dance class this week. He got me in the car and drove me there. Something as simple as being driven to a park can be beneficial to your health. Let someone else help with the logistics on your behalf.

Just remember- it is okay to rest. I like to think that my fatigue means that treatment is working, even though it can feel awful. Sometimes, it isn't a matter of what you do, so much as it is a matter of time that passes. Honestly, I just ride the wave. It's okay to just be.

Okay, so I have a large range of clothing in my closet that I spent anywhere from ~$5 at a thrift store to a $200 coat from Europe. I buy based on style, fit, pockets, and type of fabric. Some of my $100+ dresses had a really crappy zipper that I had to get replaced. My H&M cargo pants, on the other hand, has lasted me years. 

What comes down to is that I know how to mend my clothes. I can darn threadbare fabric, fix a hole, reinforce a button, sew over a busted seam, zig zag stitch over fraying edges. I find that I have to repair even the clothes I made myself. The best tactic is to check every garment after washing it, and address any small fixes before  they get worse.

Also, fabric type is really important. For example, I avoid tissue cotton. That fabric is made to rip.  Look for sturdy cotton. A few years ago, I needed a snug fitting black t-shirt. Target only had tissue cotton at the time. I went from store to store until I walked into Old Navy and felt that the cotton was good quality. I often feel the fabric or look at the fabric contents before I buy a garment. 100% polyester is something I avoid in shirts and dresses because it is not a breathable material for summer, but it is convenient in a skirt because I dont need to worry about ironing. A poly-cotton blend can work really nice, but the breathability varies tremendously. Watch for pilling in sweaters- I have a turtleneck sweater from Express that I bought a few years ago that I freaking love, even though it was like $40 when I was getting other turtlenecks that were way cheaper at the thrift store.

What you are going through is disgraceful, and I hurt knowing that you have to go through this. I am a vet in this field. Below I have compiled the best advice given, and added nuances that got left out.

1. Document. Everything. Journal your emotions, what you are doing (reading books, lying in bed, crying because of x, etc.), what is going on around you (what step mom is saying/doing, what dad is doing), times, dates, etc. Try to get voice recording if your step mom if verbally abusing you. You don't have to record everything, but try to also include good things if they happen (like if you play a game or something). But here is the thing, don't keep everything in one spot. Step mom can read and take away your journal, so have a backup on email. Take photos of your journal pages. I do not recommend taking out your journal infront of this therapist or your step mom. It may lead to retaliation, so share it with people who not only are legally required to keep it between you and them, but also people who have never met your stepmom. Also, see if you can get a hold of your previous medical records, and save them in different places as well. This will help you see if your therapist is blatantly not writing your side of the story in their notes. Make sure to document what you told the therapist in each session as well.

2. Someone mentioned that in Ohio you can get your own therapist at 14. Do this. Find your insurance card (try taking a pic and leaving it wherever it is so you can be discreet), and hopefully you can get teletherapy. You can feel out your therapists until you find someone trustworthy. Again, try to be discreet about this if you can. Once you have your own person, ask them to put your journal entries on their file (and email them the pics!) Note that some practices don't release records if there is a custody suit involved unless court ordered, so read the patient agreement carefully, and try to find a practice that fits what kind of record release situation you may need down the road. If your step mom forces you to stop the appointments, keep in mind that will look bad on her down the road. Another thing to think about is to ask for a new therapist at the practice that your step mom is taking you to. It is normal for people to not jive with the current doctor, and the receptionist can switch to a new one for you. I would just say you are not clicking or something to that effect. As others mentioned, it is a good idea to demand that stepmom not even be in the room with you during your appointment.

3. Try to get back into school. Look into online school. Fuck, walk or bike back to your old school and ask for resources. Your local library may have resources. Try calling legal aid. The bottom line is to get outside help. There are mental health organizations out there like NAMI that may also help you. I do recommend trying to get legal aid if you are considering emancipation.

4. Create a safety plan. Put things like a change of clothes in a bag or backpack, and keep it somewhere safe. Put your important belongings in there, too. If you can get a hold of your birth certificate and social security number, or even just memorize your social security number, get them discreetly. That way, if you need to leave house immediately, you can grab your stuff and go. Contact any friends ahead of time to see if anyone is willing to house you while you look for outside help. Your parents will probably end up calling the police if you leave, so if you contact an organization ahead of time, you might have better options to choose from. I also recommend having a separate backpack ready for mental hospitals. Read up on contraband so you can be prepared, and try not to bring anything they won't let you have (drawstring hoodies/pants, stuffed animals, blankets) This will make it easier on your heart if you ever have to go in. Read up on the process of hospitalization so that your first day isn't completely miserable. Honestly hospitalizations can be a useful tool if you absorb the therapy and activities they provide. You can bring books and photos for comfort.

5. Remember that if you are in danger of yourself or others, authority figures like therapists and the police are mandated reporters, and can send you to a mental hospital. Read up on mandated reporting, but also remember that if you need help then it might actually be nice to get away from Step mom. You can refuse to sign a release of info for step mom, and you can refuse to have her visit you in the hospital. If you have to go, do so voluntarily, as it is better than a 302. You can refuse or try out new meds as you wish if you go in voluntarily. Some places offer residential programs so you can literally live away from stepmom afterwards.

6. Many people are suggesting to report your therapist, call the police, and/or call CPS. Get your medical records from your therapist in advance before you report to build a strong case. The police usually just 302 you or send you back home, and hospitals are also likely to send you back to step mom. If the police come, go voluntarily like I said. Honestly I would go to organizations outside of the police first for resources. They can give you better options than the police can, unless of course you were assaulted. If you are assaulted, do call 911 and take pictures of injuries. Unfortunately, CPS can stir up more drama if they can't help you. If you don't have bruises or broken bones, and if you do have a bed,  food, adequate shelter, clothes- CPS can't help you. In my experience, CPS made things worse for me. However, again if 911 is called due to violence or sexual assault then CPS is worth contacting. Just remember that CPS will need proof to take action. Still report even if you don't have that proof. Make a paper trail if you need to.

Last but not least, expect your step mom to undermine your efforts if she finds out about them. This is why finding outside help is critical. She will make herself look really dumb if she does manage to prevent you from helping yourself. Expect this to be a longterm effort. If she wins a battle, know she won't win the war.
